diagnostic_evidence.quote: The same four equation hold if we replace $\va$ with $\matR_\va$, $\vy$ with $\matR_\vy$ and $\Mprod$ with matrix product. Thus, $\matR_\vy$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\matR_\va$.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof verifies four ring-level identities for a constructed real vector y and for a^\winv, then asserts that 'the same four equations hold' after replacing tubes by representation matrices R_x = M^{-1}diag(Mx)M, concluding that R_y and R_{a^\winv} are Moore-Penrose pseudoinverses of R_a and hence equal. The first two identities translate (x -> R_x is a ring homomorphism), but the last two would require R_{a ⋆ y} and R_{y ⋆ a} to be Hermitian (symmetric), i.e. ring conjugation to correspond to matrix transposition under x -> R_x, which fails in general. Counterexample: M = [[1,1],[0,1]] (all rows real, so a legitimate K_M), a = (1,0): then a^\winv = y = (1,0) and R_a = [[1,1],[0,0]] is not symmetric, so R_{a^\winv} violates the Moore-Penrose symmetry condition and is not the MP pseudoinverse of R_a (which is (1/2)[[1,0],[1,0]]). The uniqueness conclusion is thus unfounded. Additionally, the rules defining delta_j for a conjugate row pair (stated only for gamma_k gamma_l != 0, with l undefined) omit the cases where one or both of gamma_j, gamma_k vanish, leaving y undefined for some inputs. The lemma itself is true, since componentwise My = (Ma)^\pinv for the constructed y.

failure_location.quote: the same four equations hold with $\va^\winv$ replacing $\vy$, and similary $\matR_{\va^\winv}$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\matR_\va$. However, the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse is unique, so $\matR_{\va^\winv}= \matR_\vy$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the Moore-Penrose detour by the direct observation that the constructed y satisfies My = (Ma)^\pinv componentwise (completing the missing delta cases), whence y = a^\winv is real; this also repairs lem:added-2's reliance.
issues.overall_effect: Realness of weak inverses is left unproved as written; Lemma lem:added-2, whose statement includes a^\winv in K_M and whose proof does not re-establish realness, inherits the gap.
issues.title: Invalid Moore-Penrose uniqueness step in the proof of the weak-inverse realness lemma
issues.why_classification: The lemma and its dependent are true; a short, local rewrite of the final proof step (or the structural argument via Lemma lem:struct-Minv) preserves every substantive claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since complex rows in $\matM$ come in pairs, the parity of the realness must be equal to the parity of $n$
Consider the case \(n=2\). Since \(\R^2\) is isomorphic \(\C\) we can use the multiplication operation defined by complex numbers to get a field
which is DFT matrix for $n=2$. We see that the split-complex product is the t-product for $n=2$.

issues.failure_explanation: Admissible realness values are m with m ≡ n (mod 2) and 0 ≤ m ≤ n, i.e. exactly floor(n/2)+1 values; since the isomorphism type is determined by realness (K_M ≅ R^m x C^{(n-m)/2}), there are floor(n/2)+1 isomorphism classes of n-dimensional tubal rings, not ceil(n/2). For even n the stated formula is off by one: for n = 2 the paper itself exhibits two non-isomorphic tubal rings (complex numbers, realness 0, and split-complex/t-product, realness 2), while ceil(2/2) = 1. The claim also silently uses the unproven converse of Proposition prop:realness-iso (different realness implies non-isomorphic).

failure_location.quote: thus there are, up to isomorphism, $\lceil \nicefrac{n}{2} \rceil$ tubal rings

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the count to floor(n/2)+1 and prove the converse of Proposition prop:realness-iso (e.g. via the R^m x C^{(n-m)/2} product structure).
issues.overall_effect: The enumeration of possible tubal rings in the unavoidability discussion is wrong for every even n; no formal result depends on it.
issues.title: Incorrect count of tubal rings up to isomorphism
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the count (plus a short standard argument for the converse direction) preserves all surrounding claims.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Furthermore, it can be verified that weak inverses for non-zero elements are given by:

issues.failure_explanation: Under the stated condition a ≠ b, the element [a,-b]^T with a = -b ≠ 0 (e.g. [1,-1]^T) makes the denominator a^2 - b^2 vanish, so the first formula is undefined; no formula is given for this case. In the diagonalizing coordinates (a+b, a-b) the weak inverse of such an element is (0, 1/(2(a-b))), i.e. [1/(4a), -1/(4a)]^T, which the displayed case analysis omits. The condition on the first formula should be a^2 ≠ b^2. The example's conclusion that the split-complex numbers form a tubal ring is unaffected.

failure_location.quote: \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix}^\winv = \begin{bmatrix} a/(a^2-b^2) \\ -b/(a^2-b^2)\end{bmatrix}\,\,(\text{for }a\neq b), \quad\quad \begin{bmatrix} a \\ a \end{bmatrix}^\winv = \begin{bmatrix} 1/4a \\ 1/4a \end{bmatrix}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the condition to a^2 ≠ b^2 and add the missing case [a,-a]^T^\winv = [1/(4a), -1/(4a)]^T.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed weak-inverse formula in the split-complex example is false/incomplete for the zero-divisor line a = -b; nothing downstream relies on the exact formula.
issues.title: Wrong condition and missing case in the split-complex weak-inverse formula
issues.why_classification: A local fix of the case split in a standalone example; the substantive claim (split-complex numbers are a tubal ring) survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then there exist \(\Mprod\)-unitary tensors \(\tenU \in \KM^{m\times m}\) and \(\tenV \in \KM^{p\times p}\) and an f-diagonal tensor \(\tenS \in \KM^{m\times p}\) such that \(\tenA = \tenU \Mprod \tenS \Mprod \tenV^\ha\).
we define the transformed tensor \(\hat{\tenA}\in\C^{m\times p \times n}\) as \(\hat{\tenA} \coloneqq \tenA \nmodeprod{3} \matM\)
We can then move back to the primal domain to obtain \(\tenA = \tenU \Mprod \tenS \Mprod \tenV^\ha\).

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem claims factors in K_M^{m x m} and K_M^{p x p}, i.e. real tensors. A tensor obtained as \hat{\tenU} x_3 M^{-1} is real only if the slices of \hat{\tenU} at real rows of M are real and the slices at conjugate-paired rows are mutually conjugate. Taking 'a SVD decomposition for each frontal slice on its own' does not ensure this: SVD factors are never unique, and the SVDs of a conjugate pair of slices of \hat{\tenA} need not be chosen as conjugates of each other, so the resulting \tenU, \tenV can be complex, hence not elements of K_M^{m x m} and not ⋆_M-unitary in the defined sense. The necessary step — choosing the per-slice SVDs compatibly (real SVDs on real-row slices, conjugate SVDs on conjugate-paired slices, which is always possible since the corresponding slices of \hat{\tenA} are real or conjugate; \tenS is then real automatically) — is missing.

failure_location.quote: Construct a SVD decomposition for each frontal slices on its own, collecting the left and right unitary matrices to form $\hat{\tenU}$ and $\hat{\tenV}$ respectively, and the singular values in $\hat{\tenS}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the observation that the slices of \hat{\tenA} at real rows of M are real and at paired rows come in conjugate pairs, so the per-slice SVDs can and must be chosen conjugate to each other (and real on real rows), making \tenU, \tenS, \tenV real.
issues.overall_effect: The existence proof of the M-product-SVD, as written, does not establish the claimed membership of the factors in K_M; the theorem itself is true and the downstream Eckart-Young results are unaffected once the choice is made.
issues.title: t-SVD existence proof does not establish that the factors are real (in K_M)
issues.why_classification: The gap is closed by a standard one-sentence choice argument inside the existing proof; the statement and all dependents survive unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: By Lemma lem:added-4, ‖\hat{X}‖_F = |c|·‖X‖_F, so ‖X‖_F^2 = |c|^{-2}·‖\hat{X}‖_F^2. With the per-slice Eckart-Young identity ‖\hat{\tenA} − \widehat{\lrapprox{\tenA}{\vr}}‖_F^2 = Σ_j Σ_{i>r_j} \hat{σ}_{ij}^2, the correct formula is |c|^{-2}·Σ_j Σ_{i>r_j} \hat{σ}_{ij}^2. The stated factor |c|^{-1} is wrong whenever |c| ≠ 1 (e.g. m = p = n = 1, M = [c], \tenA = [a], r = 0: the left side is a^2 while the stated right side is |c|·a^2), and it contradicts Theorem thm:first-eckart-young combined with Corollary cor:added-1, where squared norms scale by |c|^{-2}. The optimality part of the theorem is correct.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace |c|^{-1} by |c|^{-2} in the error formula (the omitted proof, being the same as the previous theorem's, then matches the statement).
issues.overall_effect: The stated squared-error formula in the multirank Eckart-Young theorem is quantitatively wrong for every |c| ≠ 1; no labelled result depends on this formula.
issues.title: Wrong scaling constant in the multirank Eckart-Young error formula
issues.why_classification: A single-constant correction, forced by the paper's own norm-scaling lemmas, restores the theorem verbatim; the optimality guarantee is untouched.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose that $\matM=\matD\matW$ for some invertible real diagonal matrix and unitary $\matW$. Then for every $\va,\vx,\vy$ we have

We would expect that this adjoint will be given by the conjugate to $\va$, i.e., $T^\adj_\va(\vy)=T_{\va^\sconj}(\vy)=\va^\sconj \Mprod \vy$, however it is easy to build counter examples for which this does not hold. However, if $\matM$ is a scaled unitary matrix then it does hold

issues.failure_explanation: The entrywise step of the proof invokes Proposition prop:hilbert-algebra, which requires M = DW (invertible real diagonal times unitary); the statement of prop:hilbert-algebra-tensors imposes no condition on M, so as stated it is false for general tubal rings — consistent with the paper's own remark that 'it is easy to build counter examples' to the tube-level identity. Counterexample: M = [[1,1],[0,1]] (all rows real, a valid tubal-ring matrix not of the form DW since MM^T is not diagonal), \tenA = [(1,0)], \matX = e_1, \matY = e_2 as tubes: dotprod{\tenA ⋆ \matX}{\matY} = 0 while dotprod{\matX}{\tenA^\ha ⋆ \matY} = 1, because a^* = a and R_a = [[1,1],[0,0]] is not symmetric.

failure_location.quote: Suppose that $\tenA\in\KM^{m\times p}$. For every $\matX \in \KM^p$ and $\matY\in\KM^m$ we have $\dotprod{\tenA \Mprod \matX}{\matY} = \dotprod{\matX}{\tenA^{\ha} \Mprod \matY}$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis M = DW (invertible real diagonal times unitary) to the statement of prop:hilbert-algebra-tensors; the given proof then applies verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: The tensor-level Hilbert-algebra identity is asserted for all tubal rings but holds only for the DW class; the surrounding conjecture relating Hilbert structure to Eckart-Young results is framed on the unsupported generality.
issues.title: Tensor-level Hilbert-algebra proposition stated without its needed hypothesis on M
issues.why_classification: Adding the standard local hypothesis — exactly the one already present in the tube-level Proposition prop:hilbert-algebra and matching the subsection's advertised scope — preserves the result and proof.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: is called a \emph{tubal ring} if it is commutative, unital, von Neumann regular, and is also an associative algebra over \(\R\) with respect to the usual scalar-vector product.

Suppose that \((\R^n, +, \cdot)\) is a tubal ring. Then, there exists an invertible matrix \(\matM\in\C^{n\times n}\) such that for all \(\va, \vb \in \R^n\), we have \(\va \cdot \vb = \va \Mprod \vb\).

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that ⋆_M is the only way to define a ring of tubes (on R^n with the usual addition) that is commutative, unital and von Neumann regular. Theorem thm:main proves this only under the additional tubal-ring hypothesis that the ring is an associative R-algebra with respect to the usual scalar multiplication, which the parenthetical list omits. Without that hypothesis the claim is false: transporting the field C along a merely Q-linear additive automorphism of R^n yields a commutative, unital, von Neumann regular ring on R^n whose product is not R-bilinear and hence cannot equal M^{-1}(Ma ∘ Mb) for any matrix M.

failure_location.quote: The resulting product is the only way to define a ring of tubes with all the desired properties (commutative, unital and von Neumann regular).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the conclusion's uniqueness claim with the full tubal-ring hypothesis list, including compatibility of the product with the usual R-scalar multiplication.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's headline uniqueness claim is stated with an incomplete hypothesis list, claiming a stronger scope than Theorem thm:main establishes.
issues.title: Conclusion's uniqueness claim omits the R-algebra hypothesis
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence restatement of the conclusion with the hypotheses already formalized in the tubal-ring definition removes the overclaim; no formal result changes.
